title: Freedom of Religion
objective: After this level you can explain freedom of religion and belief.
summary: Freedom of religion covers belief, which can't be limited, and practice, which can be, but only for a few listed reasons. Countries arrange religion and state differently.

cards.headline: You can believe whatever you like. Acting on it is where the rules begin.
cards.body: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration gives everyone freedom of thought, conscience and religion. That includes the freedom to change your religion or belief, and to show it in teaching, practice, worship and observance. Two halves, then: what you believe, and what you do about it. International law treats them very differently.

cards.headline: Believing: no limits allowed
cards.body: The UN Human Rights Committee says no limitations are permitted on the freedom to have or adopt a religion or belief of your choice. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) adds that no one may be coerced in a way that would impair that freedom. A government can't make it illegal to believe something. Your mind is the one room it never gets a key to.

cards.headline: Practising: limits, but only a few
cards.body: Showing your religion is different, because it can affect other people. Under ICCPR Article 18, it may be limited, but only by law and only where necessary to protect public safety, order, health or morals, or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others. Think of it as a short list of permitted reasons. Any limit has to point to one of them.

mascot.line: Believing and practising are easy to blur. Belief allows no limits; practice allows a short list.

cards.headline: Three ways to arrange religion and state

items.label: United States
points: Congress may make no law establishing a religion
Nor any law prohibiting its free exercise

items.label: France
points: A 1905 law separated churches and the state
The state doesn't recognize, fund or endorse religious groups

items.label: England
points: The Church of England is the established church
The monarch is its supreme governor

cards.headline: Where's the line? A live debate
cards.body: In 2004 France banned conspicuous religious symbols, such as Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and large Christian crosses, for pupils in public schools. The Stasi Commission and President Jacques Chirac backed it as applying laïcité, France's secularism. Human Rights Watch called it an unwarranted infringement on religious practice, arguing such symbols threatened no one's safety, order or rights. Underneath sits one question: when is a limit on practice truly necessary?

cards.headline: Freedom of religion: explored
learned: Practice can be, only for a few listed reasons
US, France and England arrange religion and state differently
France's 2004 law shows where the debate lies

questions.prompt: In this level's comparison, which country has an established church with the monarch as its supreme governor?

options.label: France
options.rationale: France's 1905 law separated churches and the state.

options.label: The United States
options.rationale: The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing a religion.

questions.explanation: The Church of England is England's established church, and the British monarch is its supreme governor.

questions.prompt: Under international law, what's the key difference between holding a religion and practising it?

options.label: Practice can't be limited, but belief can
Governments may limit both whenever they wish
options.rationale: Belief can't be limited at all; practice only for listed reasons.

options.label: Belief can't be limited; practice can, for a few listed reasons
Neither one is mentioned in the Universal Declaration

questions.explanation: No limits are permitted on having or adopting a religion or belief; showing it may be limited only by law and where necessary for safety, order, health, morals or others' rights.

questions.prompt: France's 2004 school rule on religious symbols limited which side of freedom of religion?

options.label: Believing: it banned certain beliefs outright
options.rationale: It regulated symbols pupils wear, not beliefs they hold.

options.label: Changing religion: it stopped pupils converting
options.rationale: It was about symbols worn in school.

options.label: Practice: showing religion through visible symbols
Neither: it only concerned school fees
options.rationale: It concerned religious symbols in public schools.

questions.explanation: Wearing a symbol is a way of showing religion, the practice side. That's why the debate turned on whether the limit was necessary.
